preacher.name: Charles Grandison Finney
preacher.tradition: Presbyterian, later Congregationalist; Second Great Awakening revivalism (Oberlin theology)
preacher.role: Revivalist, theologian and Oberlin College president
preacher.bio: Charles Grandison Finney was born in Warren, Connecticut, on 29 August 1792. He was training in law when he experienced a religious conversion at Adams, New York, in October 1821, and he was ordained a Presbyterian minister in 1824. His revival campaigns in New York State, including Rochester in 1830–31, made him a central figure of the Second Great Awakening, and from 1832 he was a pastor in New York City, first at the Chatham Street Chapel and then at the Broadway Tabernacle. In 1835 he became professor of theology at the new Oberlin Collegiate Institute in Ohio, where he later pastored the First Congregational Church, wrote for The Oberlin Evangelist and became president in 1851; he denounced slavery from the pulpit, twice preached at length in Britain, and died at Oberlin on 16 August 1875, his Memoirs appearing in 1876.
preacher.corpus_note: Many of Finney's sermons were printed in his lifetime: in collections such as Sermons on Important Subjects (1836) and Lectures to Professing Christians (1837), in London's Penny Pulpit (1849–51), and, according to Gospel Truth Ministries, by the hundreds in The Oberlin Evangelist (1839–62), which it describes as the only source for those sermons. The Oberlin College Archives hold over six hundred of his manuscript sermon outlines (1853–75); no documented total count of his sermons was found.

sermons.title: Sinners Bound to Change Their Own Hearts
sermons.published_in: Sermons on Various Subjects (New York: S. W. Benedict, 1835; copyright entered 1834), Sermon I, there titled 'Sinners Bound to Change Their Own Heart'; reprinted as Sermon I of Sermons on Important Subjects (3rd ed., New York: John S. Taylor, 1836)
sermons.summary: Finney argues that the 'new heart' commanded in Ezekiel 18:31 is not a new soul, organ or faculty but a change in the mind's governing preference, from pursuing one's own interest to choosing God's glory and kingdom. Because sinners already have every power of moral agency, the command is reasonable; the Bible ascribes conversion to four agencies, the Spirit, the truth, the preacher and the sinner, and Finney illustrates their roles with a man turned back from the edge of Niagara Falls by a warning cry. He concludes that sinners must not wait for God to change them but must turn at once.
sermons.context: The sermon opened Finney's first sermon collection, whose copyright was entered in 1834 while he was pastor of the Second Free Presbyterian Church in New York, and it was reprinted as the first sermon of the 1836 Sermons on Important Subjects. Obbie Tyler Todd (Journal of the Evangelical Theological Society, 2020) describes it as an 1834 sermon and cites it for Finney's moral-government theology, and The American Yawp Reader reproduces an excerpt to illustrate his emphasis on human choice in salvation. Finney's Memoirs record that during his revival at Wilmington, Delaware, he preached for about two hours from this text on what a new heart was and was not; they do not say whether that sermon is the one later printed.
sermons.key_line: It is not the appropriate work of God to do what he requires of you.

sermons.title: Lectures on Revivals of Religion
sermons.place: Chatham Street Chapel, New York City
sermons.occasion: Weekly Friday-evening lectures to Finney's own congregation, reported in the New York Evangelist by its editor, Joshua Leavitt
sermons.published_in: New York Evangelist (weekly reports, 1834–35); book edition Lectures on Revivals of Religion (New York, 1835; revised edition 1868)
sermons.summary: Across 22 lectures Finney argues that a revival is not a miracle but the result of rightly using the means God has appointed, and he explains when revivals may be expected and how Christians can promote them. The lectures cover prevailing prayer, being filled with the Spirit, dealing with sinners, preaching, a defence of 'new measures' such as anxious meetings, protracted meetings and the anxious seat, hindrances to revival, and instructions for converts.
sermons.context: Finney delivered the lectures to his Chatham Street Chapel congregation during the winter of 1834–35, and Joshua Leavitt reported them for the New York Evangelist; in his Memoirs Finney says Leavitt had asked for help because the paper's subscriptions were failing. The reporter's advertisement to the book is dated April 1835, and Finney's Memoirs state that twelve thousand copies sold as fast as they could be printed and that the lectures were reprinted in England and France and translated into Welsh.
sermons.key_line: It is a purely philosophical result of the right use of the constituted means--as much so as any other effect produced by the application of means.

sermons.title: Prevailing Prayer (Lecture IV)
sermons.place: Chatham Street Chapel, New York City
sermons.occasion: Friday-evening lecture to Finney's congregation, the fourth of his Lectures on Revivals of Religion
sermons.published_in: New York Evangelist (1834–35); Lectures on Revivals of Religion (New York, 1835), Lecture IV
sermons.summary: Finney distinguishes two kinds of means in revival: truth, which acts on people, and prayer, which 'moves' God, not by changing God's mind but by bringing those who pray into the state in which God can consistently grant the blessing. He defines prevailing prayer as prayer that obtains what it seeks and lists its conditions: a definite object, agreement with God's revealed will, submission, desire proportionate to the need, right motives, the Spirit's intercession, perseverance, an agony of desire, much praying, the name of Christ, renunciation of sin, and faith.
sermons.context: This is the fourth of the revival lectures Finney gave to his Chatham Street Chapel congregation in the winter of 1834–35, reported by Joshua Leavitt in the New York Evangelist. In his 1835 preface Finney said he expected that part of the church would not understand or accept what he had taught about prayer.
sermons.key_line: Prayer is an essential link in the chain of causes that lead to a revival; as much so as truth is.

sermons.title: Why Sinners Hate God
sermons.published_in: Sermons on Important Subjects (3rd ed., New York: John S. Taylor, 1836), Sermon VI
sermons.summary: Taking Christ's words 'They have hated me without a cause', Finney argues that sinners' enmity toward God has no just ground in how God made them, in any inherited disposition, in human nature, in humanity's descent from a common ancestor, or in God's moral government. Its real cause is supreme selfishness, which God rightly opposes, so sinners hate God for the very reasons they ought to love him. In his closing remarks he says this shows what a change of heart is, makes their guilt deserving of eternal death, and will leave the saints satisfied with God's justice.
sermons.context: This is the sixth sermon in Finney's 1836 collection, and it opens by referring back to his 'two former discourses on total depravity', the fourth and fifth sermons of that volume. The edition does not record when or where it was first preached.
sermons.key_line: They do not hate him because he deserves their hatred, but because he deserves their love.

sermons.title: Christian Affinity
sermons.occasion: Preached during Finney's revival labours in Troy, soon after a session of the Presbytery of Troy opened; members of the presbytery then asked for it to be printed
sermons.published_in: First printed as 'Can Two Walk Together Except They Be Agreed?' (Troy, N.Y.: Tuttle and Richards, 1827); reprinted as 'Christian Affinity', Sermon VIII of Sermons on Important Subjects (3rd ed., New York: John S. Taylor, 1836)
sermons.summary: From Amos 3:3 ('Can two walk together except they be agreed?') Finney argues that people walk together only when their affections, not merely their opinions, agree, and that the same truth pleases or offends depending on the state of the heart. He uses this to explain why Christians of different denominations can share warm fellowship, why young converts seek one another's company, and why revivals convulse churches and why visiting ministers sometimes object to them. He concludes that sinners must be born again before they can share the company of the holy.
sermons.context: The 1827 Troy printing says the sermon was preached in the Presbyterian church at Troy on 4 March 1827. It includes a letter dated 20 March 1827 from fifteen members of the Presbytery of Troy, among them Nathan S. S. Beman, asking for a copy for the press. In his reply of 30 March, Finney says the sermon had been preached extemporaneously and that he had since hastily written down its main points. His Memoirs record that he spent the autumn and winter of 1826–27 working in a revival with Beman's church at Troy. The sermon quotes Jonathan Edwards at length on ministers who oppose a work of revival, and it was reprinted almost unchanged under the title 'Christian Affinity' in 1836.
sermons.key_line: Their differences are in a great measure lost or forgotten, while they fall in with each other's state of feeling; they will walk together while in heart they are agreed.

sermons.title: Stewardship
sermons.published_in: Sermons on Important Subjects (3rd ed., New York: John S. Taylor, 1836), Sermon IX
sermons.summary: Drawing on the parable of the unjust steward, Finney argues that God owns everything and that every person is his steward, accountable for their time, mental powers, influence, property, their own soul, the souls of others, the opinions they hold and spread, and their opportunities to do good. He presses the point with the analogy of a dishonest business agent and insists that wealth earned by one's own industry still belongs to God and must be used for the happiness and salvation of others.
sermons.context: This is the ninth sermon in Finney's 1836 collection, and its text addresses the 'reader' directly several times. No delivery date or place is recorded.
sermons.key_line: Men are mere stewards, employed by him for the transaction of his business, and required to do all they do for his glory.

sermons.title: Selfishness Not True Religion
sermons.occasion: One of Finney's Lectures to Professing Christians, reported by the editor of the New-York Evangelist
sermons.published_in: Lectures to Professing Christians (New York: John S. Taylor, 1837); Lecture III of the 1837 series
sermons.summary: Taking 'charity seeketh not her own' as his text, Finney argues that making one's own happiness the supreme aim is incompatible with true religion. He grants that a due regard for one's own welfare, according to its real value, is lawful. He then argues that supreme self-regard is contrary to the example of God and the spirit of Christ, to the law and the gospel, to conscience, reason and common sense, to the way the mind is made, and to the experience of saints. He concludes that such self-regard is selfishness, and that those who hold it while believing themselves religious are deceived.
sermons.context: In the lecture Finney says he had assumed the point was uncontroversial but had since learned that many professing Christians held a supreme regard for one's own happiness to be true religion. The Lectures to Professing Christians were delivered in New York City in 1836 and 1837. They were published in 1837 from the Evangelist editor's notes, which Finney's preface says recorded little more than a full skeleton of what he said.
sermons.key_line: He came on an errand of pure benevolence, to benefit the kingdom of God, not to benefit himself.

sermons.title: Love the Whole of Religion
sermons.occasion: One of Finney's Lectures to Professing Christians, reported by the editor of the New-York Evangelist
sermons.published_in: Lectures to Professing Christians (New York: John S. Taylor, 1837); Lecture XII of the 1837 series
sermons.summary: Finney argues that everything God requires of people is love in its various forms, distinguishing benevolence (good will toward all) from complacency (approval of good character), and love as a voluntary affection from love as an emotion. He describes what perfect love includes, such as freedom from malice and envy, supreme and disinterested love to God, and equal regard for a neighbour's interests, and what it produces, such as delight in self-denial. His closing remarks say that religious knowledge and zeal without love make people censorious and proud, and that zeal with love is not sectarian or given to controversy.
sermons.context: This lecture was delivered in New York City as part of the Lectures to Professing Christians and printed in 1837 from notes by the editor of the New-York Evangelist. In its closing remarks Finney contrasts love with church controversy, describing ministers dividing into parties at ecclesiastical meetings.
sermons.key_line: In other words, all that is required of man by God consists in love, in various modifications and results.

sermons.title: Mutual Confession of Faults, and Mutual Prayer
sermons.summary: Finney teaches that James 5:16 chiefly requires Christians to confess wrongs to the people they have injured. It also covers sharing besetting sins with trusted Christian friends so as to gain their prayers, and he rejects the view that it supports confession to priests. True confession, he argues, involves conviction, repentance, humility, readiness to make restitution and fullness. It is necessary for justice to the injured and for peace with God, with one's own conscience, with the injured person and with all the just and good. Praying for those who confess, he says, requires a real spirit of forgiveness.
sermons.context: The sermon was printed as 'Sermon by Prof. C.G. Finney. Reported by The Editor.' An editorial note says a sermon on the same text had appeared in the Evangelist's second volume and that this one was prepared independently. Gospel Truth has Finney's 'Confession of Faults' on that text from the Evangelist of 4 November 1840.
sermons.key_line: Confession is indispensable to peace with those whom we have injured.

sermons.title: The Wonderful Love of God
sermons.occasion: Sunday morning service during Finney's preaching visit to England
sermons.summary: Finney argues that God's love in giving his Son was directed to the whole human race as sinners and enemies, not to a favoured part of it. He describes this love not as approval of their character or mere emotion but as a voluntary, reasonable and unselfish good will that valued human souls, and he conveys its intensity by asking parents to imagine giving up an only child for their enemies. He then explains why such a gift was necessary and what faith is needed to receive it.
sermons.context: Finney preached this during his 1849–51 visit to England. In his Memoirs he recalls about nine months of preaching at the Tabernacle, Moorfields, a building he said held somewhat more than three thousand people, and the sermon was printed in The Penny Pulpit, a London series of sermons by various ministers.
sermons.key_line: It is plain that it was good-will, because it produced good action.

sermons.title: Repentance Before Prayer for Forgiveness
sermons.summary: Using Peter's words to Simon Magus, Finney argues that repentance is not conviction or feeling but a change of mind and will from selfishness to benevolence. It includes honesty toward God and people, confession and restitution to those who have been wronged, giving up sinful kinds and methods of business, and trust in Christ. He insists that sinners must repent before they ask for pardon. He criticises advice that tells the unrepentant to pray for repentance or for the Holy Spirit, or to wait for more conviction.
sermons.context: The sermon was printed in The Oberlin Evangelist as 'By Rev. C.G. Finney. Reported by The Editor.' It appeared after Finney's return from preaching in England (which ended in April 1851) and his election as president of Oberlin College in August 1851.
sermons.key_line: Repentance is simply and precisely a change of mind.

sermons.title: God's Love for a Sinning World
sermons.summary: Finney begins from the cost of sin under God's moral government and presents the gift of Christ as a costly, voluntary sacrifice through which God could save sinners while upholding his law. He argues that the atonement was made for the whole human race. He describes God's love not as approval of sinners or mere emotion but as a paternal, disinterested, zealous, self-denying and patient benevolence, and he sets it against what he calls the Universalist idea of mere good nature. He closes by warning that sinners may forfeit their birthright and put themselves beyond the reach of mercy.
sermons.context: The sermon was printed in The Oberlin Evangelist as 'By President Finney. Reported by The Editor', and an illustration in it refers to 'residents of Oberlin'. Finney had preached on the same verse in London in December 1850 ('The Wonderful Love of God').
sermons.key_line: Sin is the most expensive thing in the universe.

sermons.title: The Blessedness of the Merciful
sermons.summary: Finney defines mercy as treating the guilty better than they deserve. He argues that God as ruler must uphold justice, but individuals are left free to forgive their enemies and seek their good, and may not take revenge. He distinguishes this from a kind of compassion that excuses sin and shields offenders from punishment, which he links with Universalists. He insists that anyone who has not forgiven everyone from the heart is not forgiven by God. He illustrates this with a dying Black man ('a poor colored man') who at first refused to forgive those who had robbed him of his liberty and labour for most of his life, and who later said he now loved his enemies.
sermons.context: The sermon was printed in The Oberlin Evangelist ('By President Finney. Reported by The Editor') as one of a run of sermons on the Beatitudes, followed by 'Blessedness of the Pure in Heart' (1 September 1858) and 'The Blessedness of the Persecuted' (15 September 1858).
sermons.key_line: Those who have not from their hearts forgiven all men are not themselves forgiven.

sermons.title: On Love to Our Neighbor
sermons.summary: Finney defines the love owed to a neighbour as a voluntary, constant good will that values others' interests as one's own, and argues that it must reach enemies as well as friends. He treats it as the test of true humanity and true morality and as necessary for salvation and heaven. He stresses mutual obligations between God and people, children and parents, pupils and teachers, and the college and its founders and donors. In closing he applies the golden rule to slavery, asking hearers to imagine themselves and their families enslaved when deciding how to vote.
sermons.context: The sermon was printed in The Oberlin Evangelist ('By President Finney. Reported by The Editor') two weeks after 'On Loving God' (20 June 1860). It refers back to what Finney had said 'before' about the love required towards God, and its remarks address 'this Institution' and its students. The Evangelist of 1860 was also reporting Finney's preaching in England, at Bolton from December 1859 to April 1860 and in Manchester that spring and early summer, so the sermon was evidently delivered before it was printed.
sermons.key_line: Again, no man loves his friends in the sense that pleases God, unless he also truly loves his enemies.
